tells: A single system carries the whole piece: an extruded, sculpted '26' form is rebuilt in each nation's flag colours and its own cultural ornament (Mexican eagle crest, Argentine filete-style swirls, German blackletter-adjacent poster lettering).

The type changes with each country: heavy italic extruded sans for ARGENTINA, hand-lettered DIE NATIONALELF tangled in ornament, a broadcast lower-third style for the player name. The type is built into the 3D space, not laid over it.
The lighting is real. Layered relief catches rim light and occlusion, and there is material depth in the paper-cut and plaster-like layers.
The frames show choreography: a player cutout breaks through the environment, flag cloth wraps the camera, and everything resolves to the trophy locked into the '26' lockup.
There is a studio watermark, and the broadcast package logic is consistent across all the variants.
gaps: The idea is a strong broadcast system but stays within the genre (flag colours plus a number). It needs one surprising, ownable metaphor the way B has one.
The player-cutout frame is busier and more generic sports-promo than the sculpted-relief frames. It should be brought into the same material language.
The palette is dictated by the flags. A unifying grade or a signature material across nations would make it read as authored rather than assigned.

tells: The idea belongs only to this piece: the world is a clockwork map, and cities mechanically unfold out of the land. It is world-building as exposition and became culturally iconic.
Light and texture are tactile: an astrolabe sun flaring through engraved bronze bands, gears, and tilt-shift depth of field on carved wooden and metal miniatures.
Credits sit in small, restrained engraved-serif caps beside sigils, integrated into the terrain. The title lockup is set inside the armillary ring.
Choreography is evident from frame to frame: an overhead map flight, a push-in, cities rising, and a return to the sun ring as the bookend.
The palette of bronze, verdigris and parchment is deliberate and consistent.
gaps: This is the benchmark entry. The main thing to fault is that the credit type is small and conventional next to how inventive the image is.
The map frame is flatter and less lit than the miniature frames.
The final title card relies on a familiar trailer-style flare.

tells: It is a festival-titles format (an OFFF-style lockup) with studio-name cards, which is consistent with a curated multi-studio piece.
The 3D is surreal and organic, with real material variety: glass tubes, knitted mesh, fibres, ceramic hands, translucent organs, and terrain with subsurface warmth.
The palette is unusual and specific: dusty pink against basalt, sky blue with amber glass, pistachio fabric, and bottle green with jade.
Each frame is a different world rather than one layout repeated, and there is clear evidence of different hands and art directions.
gaps: The type is minimal: studio names in a default bold grotesk dropped into the corners like captions. It needs a typographic idea that ties into the forms.
There is no through-line. It is a collage of strong individual frames without the single structural idea or choreography B has.
The aesthetic (soft surreal 3D, tubes and fabric) sits close to the current festival-reel trend. It needs one image that breaks from that vocabulary.

defects: Transitions between the club shots are soft cross-dissolves. In the pairs, HARBOUR and the lighthouse show as faint ghosts over the red Northbridge plate, which looks muddy rather than like a planned match-cut.

The final lockup is cluttered. Faint dot-numerals behind the dots read as '1945', the red/teal split, the two-line team names, the league line and TONIGHT all compete in one frame. The numerals are ghosted rather than resolved or removed.
'NORTHBRIDGE CITY' is cut off at the left edge during the push into the final frame, and the motion blur on it is heavy and smeary.
The tail is static for about 4 s (change drops to 6–11 per second), so the last shot is mostly dead air.
The floodlight-and-rain opener uses a stock rain overlay that falls in straight, uniform streaks with no depth or variation in parallax.
'CITY' sits as a small, isolated corner label on the Northbridge plate, with weak hierarchy against the bridge.

The spectrogram shows noise-sweep risers, three symmetric whoosh swells and a few clicks, with no harmonic content, melody or rhythm section. It looks like synthesised filler: risers cut off abruptly at 2.5 s and 7.5 s, and the low end is static.
gaps: Choreography and arc: the energy peaks at around 4–5 s (about 45%) and then dies. A top studio would build through the club reveals into a hard collision at the centre circle at 70–80%, then land the lockup quickly and hold it for no more than 1 s. Here the shots are joined by dissolves and pushes rather than motivated match-cuts. The bridge arc could become the ball's trajectory, or the lighthouse beam could become a floodlight beam.

Sound is placeholder-grade: generic risers, whooshes and clicks with no score, no crowd, no rain bed and no designed impact on the kick-off or lockup. It has no low-end hit and no musical identity, and the dynamics are just swell-and-cut.

The finish is inconsistent. The illustration style and grain are good, but the final frame is overloaded with ghosted layers. The type is a single condensed family used without contrast in scale or rhythm. The 1945 dot-numeral device, the strongest idea in the piece, gets no payoff: it should turn on bulb by bulb to the audio, then clear before the club names arrive.
